items.item: Before Spark 4.2's named-source support, swapping which source feeds a query (even a logically equivalent replacement, like migrating from one Kafka cluster to another) was indistinguishable from an entirely different, checkpoint-breaking source to the engine -- named sources exist specifically to let such a swap happen without a full checkpoint reset.

at.out: the pre-4.2 all-or-nothing source-identity problem that named sources solve named only; this topic's own examples.py measures the 4.0.0-era restriction (changed grouping keys break restart), not the 4.2 relaxation itself

items.item: The V3 commit log that sink naming introduces in 4.2 persists which named sink produced each committed batch, which matters specifically when a query's output is later rerouted to a differently-configured sink of the same type -- without that persisted name, Spark has no way to tell a legitimate sink reconfiguration apart from an entirely different sink.

at.out: the V3 commit log's specific role in sink identity across restarts named only; this topic's own examples.py measures batchId-based sink-level dedup, not the commit log's own sink-naming mechanism

items.item: Changes to a file sink's output directory are explicitly disallowed between restarts, even though the file sink is the one sink the docs mark as exactly-once -- exactly-once accounting and checkpoint-compatibility rules are two separate axes, and a sink can be strict on one while still being restricted on the other.

at.out: output-directory changes as a separate, file-sink-specific checkpoint-compatibility restriction named only; this topic's own examples.py changes grouping keys, not a sink's output location

items.item: foreachBatch's own documentation warns it cannot be used with continuous processing mode, since that mode has no discrete batchId to key a deduplication check against -- the very mechanism this topic measures (batchId-keyed idempotent writes) is unavailable under the one execution model where micro-batch boundaries don't exist.

at.out: foreachBatch's incompatibility with continuous processing, and why, named only; this topic's own examples.py uses ordinary micro-batch execution throughout

items.item: Addition or deletion of a filter, or a same-output-schema projection change, is explicitly allowed between restarts -- a narrower, compatible category of query change that sits alongside the incompatible category (changed grouping keys, changed source count) this topic measures directly.

at.out: the compatible-change category, as the contrast to the incompatible one measured here, named only; this topic's own examples.py constructs only an incompatible change (different grouping keys)

items.item: A projection change to a different output schema is only conditionally allowed, depending on whether the sink itself can absorb the new schema -- a third category, neither flatly allowed nor flatly disallowed, that depends on a property of the sink this topic's own sink-focused claims (1 and 2) don't test for schema tolerance.

at.out: the sink-dependent, conditionally-allowed schema-change category named only; this topic's own examples.py uses a fixed schema throughout both sink probes

items.item: A stream-stream join's own equi-join columns and join type (inner vs. outer) are named explicitly among the stateful operations whose schema can't change between restarts, extending the same checkpoint-compatibility rule this topic measures on a plain aggregation to a second, more complex stateful operator from the previous two topics.

at.out: the join-specific instance of the same checkpoint-compatibility rule named only; this topic's own examples.py tests the rule on a groupBy aggregation, not a join

items.item: The Kafka sink's at-least-once guarantee means an idempotent-write strategy like this topic's batchId-based deduplication is exactly as necessary there as for the custom foreachBatch sink measured directly -- the file sink's own exactly-once guarantee is the exception among built-in sinks, not the rule.

at.out: the Kafka sink's own need for the identical idempotent-write pattern measured here on a custom sink named only; this topic's own examples.py uses a custom foreachBatch sink, not the built-in Kafka sink

items.item: foreachBatch documents a separate caveat for stateful streaming queries with multiple actions inside the same batch function: each action can trigger input data to be read and processed again, so the batch DataFrame should itself be cached inside the function to avoid silently recomputing (and potentially re-reading) the same batch's data.

at.out: the multiple-actions-inside-foreachBatch recomputation caveat named only; this topic's own examples.py performs exactly one action (collect) per batch inside each sink function

items.item: A streaming aggregation's commit-log-based recovery (this topic's claims 1 and 2) and its state-schema-based restart validation (claim 3) are enforced by two entirely separate mechanisms inside Spark -- one governs whether a specific batch gets redone, the other governs whether the restarted query is even allowed to start -- which is why a batchId-based fix for the first kind of problem does nothing to prevent the second.

at.out: the two separate enforcement mechanisms underlying claims 1-2 versus claim 3 named only; this topic's own examples.py demonstrates both mechanisms' effects directly without naming them as architecturally distinct
